docs.title: Responsible AI
docs.text:
Validation is mandatory at every level

At all proficiency levels, AI-generated outputs must be validated before use in any deliverable.

  • Check AI-generated code or logic for correctness against the business requirement
  • Do not publish, deploy, or share AI-generated results without independent review
  • Flag and escalate unexpected, incorrect, or biased outputs
  • Apply Accenture's Responsible AI principles in all AI-assisted work Document which parts of a deliverable were AI-assisted when working in regulated environments

P1–P2, validation happens with senior support. · P3 onward, independent validation is expected as standard practice. · P4 onward, you are also responsible for defining what validation looks like for your team.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Assessment RulesAssessment Process
  1. You must meet all requirements for the target level and below.
  2. Training alone does not prove proficiency.
  3. A single prototype is not enough for P4 or P5.
  4. Evidence must show both delivery and responsible execution.
  5. Real production work is preferred; realistic examples may be accepted if needed.
  6. AI-assisted work must clearly show the candidate’s decisions and corrections.
  7. Assessors may request additional evidence or a demo.
  8. Levels are based on consistent performance, not isolated examples.
  9. Platform-specific skills are assessed separately from general capability.
  1. Self-assessment — choose a level and map evidence.
  2. Evidence review — check relevance, ownership, and results.
  3. Technical discussion — explain decisions and trade-offs.
  4. Calibration — compare with similar roles and standards.
  5. Decision — confirm, adjust, or request development.
  6. Development plan — define gaps and improvement actions.
  7. Reassessment — repeat when new evidence is available.

On measurement

Assessment is not exact and requires judgement. Early evaluations are for calibration, not final classification. The goal is consistency and continuous improvement over time.

docs.title: Suggested Metrics
docs.text:
DeliveryQualityOperationsAdoption & ValueGovernance
  • Faster delivery of pipelines and features
  • Less time spent on repetitive work
  • Shorter pipeline build and change cycles
  • Better documentation and test coverage
  • More reuse of components and patterns
  • Fewer issues found after release
  • Higher success rate in data reconciliation
  • More accurate quality rules and validations
  • Fewer incidents repeating over time
  • Better accuracy in retrieval / AI outputs (when applicable)
  • Faster detection, diagnosis, and recovery of issues
  • Higher success rate of automated agents or processes
  • Lower need for manual intervention
  • Better system stability (latency, reliability, cost)
  • More active users of tools and patterns
  • Higher reuse of approved frameworks
  • Improved user satisfaction
  • Reduced manual effort (time saved)
  • Cost savings or efficiency gains

Warning

Metrics should be selected for the use case. A larger number of agents or automated actions is not, by itself, evidence of value. Value is shown by less rework, earlier detection, faster recovery, lower cost, and no loss of control.

  • Accountable ownership — each agent has a clear owner
  • Approved access — agents only use allowed data and permissions
  • Defined autonomy levels — clear boundaries of what each agent can do
  • Evaluation datasets — agents are tested and validated consistently
  • Runbooks available — operational steps are documented and usable
  • Policy compliance rate — how often agents follow rules correctly
  • Blocked or invalid actions rate — how often unsafe actions are prevented
  • Traceability — all actions can be tracked and reviewed
  • Human oversight effectiveness — quality of approvals and control checks
Initial adoption

During the initial adoption period, proficiency decisions should be treated as calibrated development assessments rather than permanent labels. The purpose of the framework is to clarify expectations, guide learning, and build trusted capability. Changes are expected once the framework is used in real assessments and real projects.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
AI Data Engineering is not defined only by the use of copilots, RAG pipelines, or generative AI tools. It is defined by the ability to combine strong data engineering foundations with AI-assisted development, intelligent and agentic data operations, governed use of data agents, deterministic validation, observability and operational ownership, measurable engineering and business outcomes, and responsible scaling from task-level assistance to enterprise capability.

The progression from P1 to P5 represents increasing autonomy, complexity, scope, impact, governance responsibility, and organisational influence.

The framework should remain evidence-based, adaptable, and continuously improved as real projects and technologies evolve.

docs.title: Domains
docs.text:
The DATC Data Platform is organised into two complementary domains that work together across the full data lifecycle, from data ingestion to business insights. Each domain has its own focus, skills, and technologies, but both are essential for successful delivery.

  • Data Engineering

    Back-end data infrastructure — pipelines, cloud platforms, data architecture, storage, governance, and AI-ready data layers.

    Data Engineers build the foundation that powers analytics, reporting, and AI applications.

    They build and maintain the data platforms and pipelines that deliver reliable, analytics-ready data.

    Primary platforms: Oracle · Snowflake · Azure Data Factory · Databricks · Microsoft Fabric · dbt

    Go →

  • Data Analytics

    Front-end data delivery — dashboards, semantic models, reporting, data visualisation, and BI architecture.

    Data Analyst transform data into business insights through reporting, dashboards, and analytics solutions.

    They own the reporting layer from requirements through design, build, and production support.

    Primary platforms: Power BI · Microsoft Fabric · DAX · Power Query · Tableau · AWS QuickSight

    Go →

How the domains connect

Data Engineering builds the data layers that Analytics consumes. A semantic model in Power BI is only as good as the pipeline feeding it. Both domains collaborate on data model alignment, refresh strategy, and AI-ready data architecture.

docs.title: Data Analytics
docs.text: The Data Analytics domain covers front-end data delivery within the DATC Data Platform. Practitioners in this domain develop, migrate, deploy, and maintain data-driven insight interfaces that drive adoption and decision-making. They build scalable BI architecture, translate complex data into actionable stories, and integrate security and data privacy into reporting systems.

    Develop and maintain commercial and bespoke knowledge engine interfaces. Build open BI architecture for cross-enterprise visibility. Design and implement scalable reporting systems from requirements through production support.

  • Enterprise BI Architecture

    Design and implement systems and frameworks for collecting, managing, analyzing, and visualizing data at enterprise scale. Build robust, maintainable infrastructure to support BI initiatives across organizations.

  • Semantic Modeling

    Build and govern the semantic layer between raw data and front-end reports. Define KPI frameworks, metric hierarchies, Row Level Security, and data governance within the BI layer.

docs.title: Data Engineering
docs.text:
The Data Engineering is the discipline responsible for building and maintaining the data infrastructure that powers analytics, reporting, and AI systems.

It focuses on designing, implementing, and operating reliable data pipelines, storage systems, and processing workflows that ensure data is available, accurate, and usable across the organization.

Data Engineering acts as the foundation of the data platform, connecting raw data sources to analytics and AI-ready datasets.

AI tools and data agents increasingly support engineering tasks by accelerating development and automation. However, engineers remain fully accountable for data correctness, governance, security, and production reliability

AI extends this domain rather than replacing it. AI assistants accelerate engineering work, and data agents — goal-driven systems that use metadata, lineage, policies, and approved tools to perform or coordinate data work — are becoming the most relevant AI capability for Data Engineering. The engineer remains accountable for correctness, security, reliability, and business fitness of every data product, regardless of whether an artefact was written by hand, generated by an assistant, or produced by an agent.

docs.title: Core Responsibilities of Data Engineering
docs.text:
• Data Engineering

    Designs, builds, and maintains data pipelines and platforms that enable reliable data movement from source systems to analytics and AI layers. Owns ingestion, transformation, and delivery across the full ETL/ELT lifecycle.

  • Data Architecture

    Defines how data is structured, stored, and integrated across systems. Includes Data Vault, star schemas, lakehouse and hybrid architectures for scalable data platforms.

  • Modern Data Management & Governance

    Ensures data quality, security, lineage, and compliance across the entire data lifecycle. Implements metadata management, cataloging, and data observability.

  • AI-Ready Data

    Builds data foundations for AI and GenAI use cases such as RAG pipelines, embeddings, vector databases, and semantic layers. Ensures data is structured, clean, and trusted for AI consumption.

  • Data Agents & Agentic Data Operations

    Develops and governs AI agents that support data engineering tasks such as data profiling, SQL/pipeline generation, data quality validation, lineage analysis, incident investigation, and optimization. All agent actions are controlled through governance, approval flows, and full auditability.

  • DataOps & Platform Automation

    Automates deployment and operations of data systems using CI/CD, infrastructure-as-code, testing, monitoring, and observability. Extends automation to AI-assisted and agent-driven workflows while ensuring control, traceability, and reliability.

docs.title: Data Agents in Data Engineering
docs.text: Data agents are the AI capability most directly relevant to this domain. They are not chatbots and not simple copilots: an agent receives an engineering objective, plans the steps, calls approved tools, validates intermediate results, and either completes the task or escalates to a human.

docs.title: Agent Autonomy Tiers
docs.text:
The required level of control depends on the impact and reversibility of the action, not on the seniority of the engineer.

Tier Behaviour Data Engineering Example Required Control A0 — Inform Explains or summarizes Explain why a load failed User reviews the output A1 — Recommend Proposes an action Recommend data-quality rules Human decides A2 — Draft Produces an artefact Generate a dbt model or ADF configuration Code review + automated tests A3 — Execute with Approval Acts only after sign-off Apply an approved metadata or catalogue update Approval, logging, rollback A4 — Bounded Execution Acts within strict limits Retry eligible failed loads within a defined window Policy limits, monitoring, rollback A5 — High Autonomy Coordinates cross-system actions Autonomous workload optimization Exceptional governance + explicit authorization

docs.title: Non-Negotiable Controls
docs.text:
Every data agent in production must have:

  • a documented objective and scope;
  • an accountable human owner;
  • least-privilege data and tool access;
  • deterministic validation of its output (tests, reconciliation, schema checks);
  • logging of prompts, tool calls, approvals, and resulting data changes;
  • defined escalation conditions;
  • monitoring for success rate, failure rate, latency, and cost;
  • a tested rollback or recovery path for any write action.

Design principle

If a task can be solved reliably with deterministic automation, use deterministic automation. Agents are for tasks that require interpretation, context, planning, or tool selection — not for replacing a scheduled job that already works.

docs.title: Proficiency Assessment & Evidence
docs.text:
Training demonstrates preparation. Delivered work and evidence demonstrate proficiency.

Courses, certifications, and self-assessments support development plans. They do not by themselves establish a level. The assessment answers a practical question: what has this person actually built, validated, and owned — and at what scope?

docs.title: Accepted Evidence
docs.text:
• source code, pull requests, and code reviews;
  • pipeline and data model implementations;
  • automated test suites and reconciliation results;
  • technical designs and architecture documents;
  • agent configurations, guardrails, and evaluation reports;
  • observability dashboards, logs, and monitoring evidence;
  • deployment records and CI/CD pipelines;
  • performance before/after measurements;
  • incident reports and root-cause analyses;
  • runbooks and operational documentation;
  • reusable patterns, templates, or frameworks with proof of adoption;
  • peer, SME, architect, security, or stakeholder validation;
  • mentoring and coaching outcomes.

Client-confidential evidence must be redacted or reviewed through an approved restricted process.

docs.title: Evidence Quality Criteria
docs.text: Evidence should be recent, relevant to the claimed level, attributable to the individual, independently reviewable, supported by observable outcomes, and compliant with security and confidentiality requirements.

docs.title: Assessment Rules
docs.text:
1. A candidate must meet the expectations of the claimed level and all levels below it.
  2. Course completion alone never establishes a level.
  3. Tool familiarity is not the same as engineering or architecture proficiency.
  4. One successful prototype does not demonstrate platform- or domain-level capability.
  5. Evidence must show both delivery and validation — what was built and how it was proven correct.
  6. For AI-assisted work, the engineer's own decisions, review, and corrections must be visible.
  7. Production evidence is preferred; production-representative evidence is acceptable where access is restricted.
  8. The level reflects consistently demonstrated capability, not a single exceptional example.
  9. Platform-specific expertise is assessed separately from transferable engineering capability.
  10. Assessors calibrate across the team to keep levels comparable.

docs.title: Assessment Process
docs.text:
1. Self-assessment — the engineer proposes a level and maps evidence to each dimension.
  2. Evidence review — the assessor checks ownership, recency, scope, validation, and outcomes.
  3. Technical discussion — the engineer explains design decisions, trade-offs, controls, and limitations.
  4. Demonstration where relevant — a walkthrough of the solution or agent, including failure handling.
  5. Calibration — comparison with peers at the same claimed level.
  6. Decision — confirmed, provisionally confirmed, or development required.
  7. Development plan — gaps converted into assignments, mentoring, and learning.
  8. Periodic review — revisited when responsibilities or evidence materially change.

On measurement

Measuring competency reliably is the hardest part of this framework, and the first cycles should be treated as calibration rather than final judgement. The purpose is to make expectations explicit, give people a concrete path, and improve the model based on how it behaves in real assessments.

docs.title: Suggested Metrics
docs.text: Metrics support the assessment; they do not replace judgement. Select what fits the solution.

docs.title: Delivery & Quality
docs.text: Metric What it indicates Pipeline lead time Speed from requirement to production Deployment frequency Maturity of CI/CD and automation Test coverage Confidence in change safety Reconciliation success rate Data correctness Defect leakage to production Effectiveness of validation Documentation coverage Maintainability and knowledge transfer

docs.title: Reliability & Cost
docs.text: Metric What it indicates Pipeline success rate Operational stability Mean time to detect / diagnose / recover Observability and support quality Incident recurrence Quality of root-cause fixes Compute and storage cost per workload Platform efficiency

docs.title: Data Agents
docs.text:
Metric What it indicates Agent success rate Reliability of the agent Validation pass rate Trustworthiness of output Human-approval and escalation rate Appropriateness of the autonomy tier Rollback rate Safety of write actions Unapproved action attempts Effectiveness of guardrails Manual effort avoided Real productivity value Issues detected earlier Preventive value Accountable-owner coverage Governance completeness

Warning

A higher number of agents or automated actions is not evidence of maturity. Value is demonstrated by outcomes: less rework, earlier detection, faster recovery, lower cost, and no loss of control.

docs.title: Framework Governance
docs.text:
This framework is expected to change as it is used.

Review triggers: after the first assessment cycle · when platform capabilities change materially · when new security, privacy, or client requirements emerge · when assessors interpret levels inconsistently · at least annually.

Owners maintain: level definitions · evidence examples · assessor guidance · calibration sessions · the training and certification catalogue (kept separate so it can be refreshed without rewriting the career model).

Each version records: version number · date · owner · approver · change summary · next review date.

Initial adoption

In the first cycles, treat proficiency decisions as calibrated development assessments rather than permanent labels. The framework exists to clarify expectations, guide learning, and build trusted capability — and it should be adjusted once real assessments show where it works and where it does not.
